summary: Defines the codecs and profiles parameters for media types that can contain several formats, such as media container types. They let a receiver tell from the Content-Type alone whether it can play the content, which helps devices with limited resources or bandwidth.

eli5.summary: A package of media might hold different kinds of sound and video. This adds a label that lists what is inside, so your device can tell before downloading if it can play it.

questions: how to declare codecs in content-type
what is the codecs parameter in content-type
what is the profiles parameter for mp4
subtitle: Two optional labels on a media Content-Type that say which codecs and profiles are inside a container file.

tldr.problem: Types such as video/mp4 or audio/3gpp are containers that can hold many different codecs, so a receiver cannot tell from the Content-Type whether it can play the content without inspecting the media itself.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6381 defines an optional 'codecs' parameter that lists every codec used, and an optional 'profiles' parameter that lists the profiles or brands the whole container claims to follow.
tldr.outcome: A server or a device with limited resources can decide to accept, reject, transcode or fetch codecs from the Content-Type alone. The RFC obsoletes RFC 4281 and adds the 'profiles' parameter.

facts.label: AVC second element
facts.value: profile_idc, constraint_set flags byte, level_idc (3 bytes in hex)

today: RFC 6381 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 4281 and updates RFC 3839, RFC 4337 and RFC 4393.

sections.title: The Problem with Bucket Types
sections.content:
MIME lets a message part declare its media type, but some type and subtype pairs are "buckets": they can contain several different formats. For example, video/3gpp may hold H.263 Profile 0, H.263 Profile 3, H.264 or MPEG-4 Simple Profile video, and several audio formats. A receiver that sees only the type knows it has a container. It does not even know whether video/3gpp content really contains video.

Without extra information, someone has to examine each media element. Reading header information is cheaper than reading everything, but it still needs specialized knowledge of each format and is resource consuming.

The RFC names two groups who feel this most. Multimedia Messaging (MMS) servers must examine the media in every message to decide whether it needs transcoding before it goes to the handset. Smart clients on devices with constrained memory, processing power or bandwidth, such as cellular telephones and PDAs, want to know in advance whether they can render a message.
sections.eli5: A lunchbox might hold a sandwich, fruit or both, and the lid does not tell you which. Someone has to open every box to find out. A label on the lid would save that work.

sections.title: The 'codecs' Parameter
sections.content:
The codecs parameter is added to the Content-Type so that all codecs needed to render the content of the MIME part are named unambiguously. It is optional in all existing types it is added to, and future types that contain ambiguity are strongly encouraged to include it. It applies to ISO Base Media File Format family files and the QuickTime file format, which covers audio/3gpp, video/3gpp, audio/3gpp2, video/3gpp2, audio/mp4, video/mp4, application/mp4, video/quicktime and application/mp21.

The value is a single value or a comma-separated list. Each value has one or more dot-separated elements. The first element's name space is set by the MIME type, and each later element's name space is set by the element before it. A list containing commas must be enclosed in quotes.

When the parameter is used it MUST list all codecs indicated by the content, and MUST NOT list any codec that no media element uses. Encoders must be complete in breadth (every four-character code in every track, for ISO family files), but receivers MUST NOT rely on the values being complete in depth, because the rules for a code may have been written after a server was implemented.

The body part is definitive. The parameter is informative. A receiver that finds extra codecs listed SHOULD discard the parameter; one that finds codecs missing MAY discard it.

Not every listed codec is always required to play the content. Alternative tracks, such as English and Spanish audio, or droppable timed text, may mean a receiver can cope with an unsupported codec after examining the media elements.
sections.eli5: The label lists every kind of food in the lunchbox, and it must not list anything that is not there. If the label and the box ever disagree, trust the box.

sections.title: Syntax and Encoding of the Value
sections.content:
The parameter has two forms. The simple form is codecs= followed by a value with no octets that need encoding. The second form, codecs*=, uses the encoding of RFC 2231 so that any octet can appear: each such octet is written as a percent sign and two hexadecimal digits, and the percent sign, asterisk and single quote characters must themselves be percent encoded. With either form, quotes allow commas and other characters in tspecials, and quotes MAY be used even when not required.

The value does not contain text for people, so the language element SHOULD be omitted, and so should the character set. A receiver MAY ignore language and MAY support only US-ASCII and UTF-8. Implementations MUST NOT add comments or folding white space between tokens except after a comma. The dot is reserved as the hierarchy delimiter.

The RFC gives these generic examples:

  • codecs=a.bb.ccc.d
  • codecs="a.bb.ccc.d, e.fff"
  • codecs*=''fo%2e
  • codecs*="''%25%20xz, gork"
sections.eli5: The label has a plain way to write the list and a fancy way for when the words contain odd characters. Both mean the same thing.

sections.title: The ISO Media Name Space
sections.content:
For ISO Base Media File Format and QuickTime files, the first element of a value is a sample description entry four-character code registered with the MP4 Registration Authority. Values are case sensitive. A file can have several tracks and each can carry several sample entries.

If the first element is mp4a (MPEG-4 audio), mp4v (MPEG-4 part-2 video) or mp4s (MPEG-4 Systems streams), the second element is the hexadecimal ObjectTypeIndication, written without the leading 0x. For mp4a with OTI 40, the third element is the audio object type in decimal, so AAC low complexity (value 2) is mp4a.40.2. For mp4v with OTI 20, the third element is the video ProfileLevelIndication in decimal, so MPEG-4 Visual Simple Profile Level 0 (value 9) is mp4v.20.9.

For the AVC family (avc1, avc2, svc1, mvc1, mvc2), the second element is the hexadecimal form of three bytes from the sequence parameter set: profile_idc, the byte holding the constraint_set flags, and level_idc. The sample entries avc1 and avc2 do not prove the media holds only AVC NAL units, since it may be SVC or MVC, which is why profile_idc is needed. When SVC or MVC content is coded in an AVC-compatible way and has two configuration records, it is recommended to report both, so the sample description code such as avc1 appears twice.
sections.eli5: Each kind of food has a short code, and the code can be followed by extra numbers that say exactly which recipe it is, like a sandwich code followed by the kind of bread.

sections.title: Examples and Extending the Parameter
sections.content:
The RFC lists Content-Type examples such as video/3gpp2; codecs="sevc, s263" (EVRC audio plus H.263 video) and video/mp4; codecs="avc1.640028" (H.264/AVC video, High Profile, Level 40). Another shows SVC video with an AVC base layer, and another shows MVC video with a High Profile base layer.

The parameter MAY be specified for additional media types. Where the ISO name space is enough, the media type registration only needs to cite this document. Where it must be expanded, a new document MAY update this one, and for non-ISO file formats a new document MAY define the name space. Extra media details such as pixel counts or color depth can be carried with the content-features header of RFC 2912.
sections.eli5: The RFC shows sample labels, like a lunchbox marked with a sandwich code and a fruit code. Other kinds of boxes can get their own label rules later.

sections.title: The 'profiles' Parameter
sections.content:
Some media files, like some codecs, can be profiled: they conform to named subsets of functionality. A profile of the container may restrict the container features, which codecs may be present, and even their profiles. The profiles parameter reports only the profiles that apply to the complete container. Profiles of the contained media are reported in codecs.

It is optional and applies to box-structured files that begin with a box of compatibility brands registered with the MP4 Registration Authority, such as a filetype or segment-type box. It is used with the same media types as codecs, apart from application/mp4. It follows the same profiles or profiles* and comma-list rules as codecs.

For files carrying MP4RA-registered brands, the parameter MUST list exactly the major brand followed by the compatible brands from the ftyp or styp box. The major brand MUST be first and MAY be removed from the compatible list. An example is profiles="mp41,isom,qvXt". As with codecs, the body part is definitive and the parameter is informative.
sections.eli5: Besides listing the foods, a second label says which rulebook the whole box follows, so you know what kind of box it is without checking each item.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The codecs parameter does not change the security considerations of the media types it is used with. An incorrect value could make content reach a device that cannot render it, or stop it reaching a device that could, so it can enable some denial-of-service attacks. The RFC says this is most likely to happen by accident, because an attacker who can alter data in transit could do more harm by altering the media itself or the content type header.

If a receiver reacts to an unsupported codec by fetching and installing it, that reaction needs to be done carefully and in accord with the system's normal validity and security checks.
sections.eli5: A wrong label could make the wrong box go to the wrong person. If your device goes and fetches a missing ingredient because of a label, it should be careful about where it gets it.

sections.title: Differences from RFC 4281
sections.content:
RFC 6381 keeps the codecs parameter of RFC 4281 in a backwards compatible way with minor clarifications. The changes it lists are:

  • a better introduction and supporting text, and better references;
  • clearer wording about which MIME types the parameters apply to, and the resulting IANA actions;
  • the new profiles parameter;
  • a fix to the BNF, which did not match the examples or common usage;
  • sub-parameters for the AVC family of codecs;
  • a security consideration for possible triggering of downloads.
sections.eli5: This is the second edition of the label rules. It fixes a mistake in the old one and adds the new rulebook label.

data.title: Content-Type with codecs
data.code:
Content-Type: video/3gpp2; codecs="sevc, s263"
Content-Type: audio/3gpp; codecs=samr
Content-Type: video/3gpp2; codecs="mp4v.20.9, mp4a.E1"
Content-Type: video/mp4; codecs="avc1.640028"
